definition: Credit-claiming occurs when a senator presents themself as responsible, in whole or in part, for obtaining, creating, advancing, protecting, or delivering a concrete governmental action, policy, funding award, program, or benefit.
clarification: I classified a release as credit-claiming when it explicitly attributes a tangible result to the senator's action, such as saying the senator authored or introduced an enacted measure, secured funding, obtained agency action, negotiated a provision, or successfully intervened for constituents. Claims can be shared with colleagues and can concern committee, appropriations, oversight, or constituent-service work. A senator's clear claim of having created or passed the underlying program also counts when the release announces benefits flowing from it.

positive_examples.text: “Dorgan authored legislation, which was signed into law, that created the National Center designation.”
positive_examples.explanation: This directly attributes the institutional designation to Dorgan's own enacted legislation.

positive_examples.text: “Sen. Talent ... announced that the Senate has approved his request for $1.5 million dollars for the Health Sciences Research and Education Facility.”
positive_examples.explanation: Talent explicitly claims responsibility for securing a specific appropriation.

positive_examples.text: “Last month, the Senate unanimously approved an amendment offered by Senators Bayh and Richard Durbin ... that would help end the Patriot Penalty.”
positive_examples.explanation: The release identifies Bayh as an author of a successfully adopted amendment with a concrete benefit.

negative_clarification: I did not classify statements as credit-claiming when they only announce an agency grant or decision without asserting the senator caused it; express support, opposition, concern, or a vote; request future action; praise another official; or commemorate an event or person. Merely sponsoring or cosponsoring a bill that has not yet produced a result is generally advocacy rather than credit for an accomplishment.

negative_examples.text: “Judge Chertoff comes to this position with a great deal of experience ... I look forward to working with Judge Chertoff.”
negative_examples.explanation: This is praise for a confirmed official and a statement of future cooperation, not a claim of achievement.

negative_examples.text: “I voted in support of the Sens. Kerry and Levin amendments today because our nation needs a plan...”
negative_examples.explanation: The senator explains a policy vote but does not claim the amendments passed or that he delivered a result.

negative_examples.text: “Senator Shelby ... announced that the Department of Homeland Security will release $3,510 to the Homewood Fire Department.”
negative_examples.explanation: The release simply reports an agency award and does not say Shelby secured, requested, or otherwise caused it.
